summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory where local legislation governs. United Kingdom law, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code, does not extend automatically and could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not covered, leaving trans people without statutory protection against discrimination. The sources identify no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery.

Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult. In 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as the "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities.

Same-sex marriage has been unavailable since 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case; the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no marital recognition.

Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to remove two Criminal Code sections, following prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex; lesbian activity was never illegal. As of 2022 the age of consent remains unequal at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 versus 16 for other sexual activity, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (the Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, 12 July) as "incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre". The 1994 decriminalisation debate likewise split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

Same-sex couples may adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015. The Bermuda Regiment officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers, though such conduct has been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists".

Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise for women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to appeal an unconstitutional case against a man charged and threatened with jail under the "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn.
tangentialFactors:
Bermuda's legal trajectory on sexual-orientation issues shows a pattern of gains reversed by legislature or apex court: marriage equality granted in 2017, revoked by statute in 2018, restored by domestic courts in 2018, then permanently barred by the Privy Council in 2022 with retrospective backdating. A trans visitor should not assume that a favourable lower-court ruling signals durable protection.

Religious institutions are an organised political force in Bermuda, staging marches against decriminalisation in 1994 and publicly condemning visible same-sex couples as recently as the Norwegian Dawn protest. This is context for the absence of gender-identity protections in the Human Rights Act.

The Bermuda Regiment conscripts by random lottery and officially prohibits anti-LGBT harassment, yet a conscript's account describes it as "the most homophobic environment that exists" with officers tolerating such conduct. Official policy and lived practice diverge.

Whether the Equality Act 2010 or any UK instrument has been extended to Bermuda by Order in Council is not addressed in this inventory beyond the general statement that UK law does not extend automatically.
